source_end_check: Recognise an emotion and healthy ways to manage stress in a fictional case.
timing: Settle, show private help route; choose matching or word finding.
Read outcome; distinguish emotion, stress and helpful action.
Model A; choose two steps or improve advice.
Check help-seeking and strategy limits; choose main task and response mode.
Case map B or advice note C, with book, typing, aid or scribe.
Check a response or repair a missing link; one next step and reply.
Explain a strategy or correct a myth.
source_timing: No fixed lesson minutes in row 64. Owner specifies 40 minutes. Brief pauses and processing time sit within the phases.

routes.Supported: Choose either main task. Read one part at a time with the word bank, sentence starters and A model. Offer a narrowed strategy menu when needed. Allow pointing, an aid or exact scribing. Record answer cues separately from usual access.
routes.Independent: Choose either main task and supply the emotion clue, two suitable strategies with reasons and help route. Keep the word bank, model and normal reading/typing aids available.
routes.Aspire: Choose either main task. Explain which strategy fits first and why another may be needed. State a limit: a strategy may help without removing the pressure or feeling at once. No personal disclosure or extra public speaking.

choices.label: Case map
choices.task: Make a case map with an emotion and clue, two healthy strategies with reasons, and a private help route.

choices.label: Advice note
choices.task: Write an advice note to the fictional young person with an emotion and clue, two healthy strategies with reasons, and a private help route.

phase_choices: Match emotion words to two quotes.
Find and label the emotion words in the quotes.
Choose two useful steps for A and give reasons.
Improve an unhelpful advice line for A with two useful steps.
Check work with the four-part list.
Find and improve one missing link in a model.
Explain why one healthy strategy may help.
Correct a myth about help and stress.
strategies: Split a task and choose a first step.
This can make a large task feel more manageable.
Take a short pause with support and a plan to return.
This gives time before trying the next step.
Ask a trusted adult for help with the pressure.
The adult can help adjust the task or find more support.
List the steps or practise one line in private.
This can make an unclear start easier to follow.
colour_blind_safe: Words, numbered cards and clear text carry all meaning. No colour-only answer codes.

cases.title: Several tasks at once
cases.text: A young person has three short tasks to finish. They say, “I feel worried. I do not know where to start.” They keep reading the list but have not chosen a first step.
cases.clue: I feel worried. I do not know where to start.
cases.pressure: Several tasks feel hard to organise.
options: A short first step can make the task clearer.
The adult can help agree which task comes first.

cases.title: Too many steps
cases.text: A young person gets several instructions at once. They say, “I feel frustrated. I keep missing a step.” They want to finish the task but are not sure which instruction comes next.
cases.clue: I feel frustrated. I keep missing a step.
cases.pressure: Several instructions are hard to follow at once.
options: Ask for one instruction at a time
This can reduce the amount to hold in mind.
A pause with a return plan can give time to settle and ask for the next step.

cases.title: Explaining a project
cases.text: A young person will explain a project to a small group. They say, “I feel worried about speaking. I cannot choose my first sentence.” They know the project facts but need a way to begin.
cases.clue: I feel worried about speaking. I cannot choose my first sentence.
cases.pressure: Starting to speak to a group feels hard.
options: Write and rehearse one opening line
A prepared first line can make the start clearer.
Ask a trusted adult for support
The adult can help agree a suitable way to take part, such as a typed response.

private_help_route: Ask a trusted adult privately or use the school’s help route. A learner may point to HELP, write a short request or say “Can we talk in private?” They need not explain to the group. If the first adult is busy or support is not enough, use the route to another trusted adult. No requirement to try every strategy before asking. Offer pass, a supported pause and a neutral task with a return plan.
typed_and_scribed_routes: For either main choice, open the editable Evidence Sheet and use the optional Type instead page. Type in the blank fields or write the advice note below the prompts. Use the usual save routine with the lesson code and work reference. Show the response privately. No login or online sharing is required. A scribe captures exact words/selections, reads back quietly and allows correction.
worked_example_and_fade: A: worried is stated in the quote. Three tasks create an organising pressure. Model one small first step and asking a trusted adult to agree priorities. Explain the reason for each. Then offer guided choice: choose two useful steps for A, or improve “Just do all three at once” using two helpful steps. Keep the model but reduce answer cues.
adaptations: Cognition and Learning: break down the case, keep a visible model and checklist. Communication and Interaction: literal words, quiet rehearsal, wait time and an aid. SEMH: predictable sequence, two choices, pass/pause and supported return. Sensory and Physical: clear print, usual aids and comfortable response position. EAL: word meanings, read together and plan in any language. Colour carries no answer meaning.
misconceptions: “Worried means weak”: emotions are not a character grade. “Everyone shows stress the same way”: one behaviour does not establish the cause. “A pause fixes everything”: it may help when agreed with a next step; task changes or more support may still be needed. “Help is only for later”: it is available while feelings are present.

main_hinge.claim: Help is available while the person still feels stressed.

parallel_hinge.claim: A strategy may help but more support may be needed.

success: Recognise a plausible emotion using a story clue.
Identify two healthy strategies and explain how each fits the pressure.

evidence.description: Dated case map for B or advice note for C: emotion and clue, two healthy strategies with reasons, and private help route. Keep actual access, answer prompts, first response, one next step and reply.

assessment: Secure: a plausible emotion supported by the case, two suitable healthy strategies with reasons, and recognition of a private route. For the exact outcome, judge emotion recognition and healthy strategy recognition separately. Help-route knowledge is recorded alongside them. Partial: feeling without clue, or strategy without fit/reason. Unobserved: no response collected, including a pass. Do not grade a learner’s own feelings or claim real-world coping from a fictional task.
where_this_leads: This helps me recognise pressure, choose a useful next step and ask for support in learning or future work.

pupil_text: INPUT
Our learning
Recognise emotions and healthy ways to manage stress.
An emotion is how a person feels.
Stress is a response to pressure.
One sign alone cannot tell us why a person feels this way.
Healthy ways support wellbeing and keep people safe.
A useful step may help. More support may still be needed.
slides.notes:

paragraphs_in_document_order: Emotions and ways to manage stress
Wednesday 6 January 2027 · P3 · 40 minutes · Year A
GROW · up to five learners · Spring 1 Week 1 · formative
Theme: Resilience & Change. Six weeks, 4 January–12 February 2027. Week 6 is assessing.
Thread tags: SMSC S/So (M/C: none); British Values IL/MR (D/RL/T: none).
Recognise emotions and healthy ways to manage stress.

Source: GROW Weekly - Spring, row 64, B64 Spr1·W1 and C64 outcome. The owner’s PSHE line sits within the generic PSHE & Citizenship heading. Named alignments and resources in A64/D64/E64/F64 are not reproduced.

Recognise a stated emotion using a story clue; identify two healthy ways to respond to the pressure and explain how each may help; identify a private help route. Choice 1 is a case map for B. Choice 2 is an advice note for C. Both meet the same checks. Offer typing for either choice.

Books, pens, Support Cards, Vocabulary Mat and an adult evidence record. Offer an editable copy of the Evidence Sheet for the optional Type instead route. Keep its typed page on screen; printed pupil pages are references, not write-on worksheets. No internet, account or pupil phone is needed. Check the actual school help route and a supported pause space. All questions and feedback are private.

Stress is a response to pressure; emotion words describe how a person feels. One sign or behaviour does not diagnose stress or a condition. Use the fictional words, not guesses from appearance. Healthy strategies protect the person and others, allow support and address the pressure where possible. They may help; none is a guaranteed cure. No personal-disclosure prompts, clinical checklist or forced calming exercise.
This helps me recognise pressure, choose a useful next step and ask for support in learning or future work.
Settle, show private help route; choose matching or word finding.
Read outcome; distinguish emotion, stress and helpful action.
Model A; choose two steps or improve advice.
Check help-seeking and strategy limits; choose main task and response mode.
Case map B or advice note C, with book, typing, aid or scribe.
Check a response or repair a missing link; one next step and reply.
Explain a strategy or correct a myth.
Total 40 minutes. Brief pauses and processing time sit inside the phases. Reduce repeated examples when extra access time is needed. No time is added for optional slide 11 or hidden staff slide 12.

Read two fictional quotes: “I feel worried about starting” and “I feel frustrated when steps are unclear”. Choose matching the two words to the quotes or finding and labelling the feeling words. Pointing, a book or typing is valid. Do not ask how anyone in the class feels.

A: worried is stated in the quote. Three tasks create an organising pressure. Model one small first step and asking a trusted adult to agree priorities. Explain the reason for each. Then offer guided choice: choose two useful steps for A, or improve “Just do all three at once” using two helpful steps. Keep the model but reduce answer cues.

Both main choices require emotion/clue, two strategies/reasons and a private route. Learners may change choice without penalty. Offer Type instead aloud and on paper. Review choice: use the four-part checklist, or improve the model “They feel bad. Take a break” by adding a precise clue or reason. Give one NS and retain the response.

Choose either main task. Read one part at a time with the word bank, sentence starters and A model. Offer a narrowed strategy menu when needed. Allow pointing, an aid or exact scribing. Record answer cues separately from usual access.
Choose either main task and supply the emotion clue, two suitable strategies with reasons and help route. Keep the word bank, model and normal reading/typing aids available.

Choose either main task. Explain which strategy fits first and why another may be needed. State a limit: a strategy may help without removing the pressure or feeling at once. No personal disclosure or extra public speaking.

Main: A the person must stop feeling stressed before asking for help; B the person can ask while still feeling stressed. Key B. Parallel: A a strategy may help but more support may be needed; B one strategy always removes stress. Key A. Accept a point, word, typed answer or scribed explanation privately. If unsure, re-model A’s help request and limit before the main task.

Cognition and Learning: break down the case, keep a visible model and checklist. Communication and Interaction: literal words, quiet rehearsal, wait time and an aid. SEMH: predictable sequence, two choices, pass/pause and supported return. Sensory and Physical: clear print, usual aids and comfortable response position. EAL: word meanings, read together and plan in any language. Colour carries no answer meaning.

Prompt ladder: 1 point to place/instruction; 2 ask a short question privately; 3 rephrase; 4 offer scaffold/choice; 5 model the first step only, then return the task. Log content help. Normal typing, reading or scribing access does not reduce independence of thought.

Ask a trusted adult privately or use the school’s help route. A learner may point to HELP, write a short request or say “Can we talk in private?” They need not explain to the group. If the first adult is busy or support is not enough, use the route to another trusted adult. No requirement to try every strategy before asking. Offer pass, a supported pause and a neutral task with a return plan.

For either main choice, open the editable Evidence Sheet and use the optional Type instead page. Type in the blank fields or write the advice note below the prompts. Use the usual save routine with the lesson code and work reference. Show the response privately. No login or online sharing is required. A scribe captures exact words/selections, reads back quietly and allows correction.

Secure: a plausible emotion supported by the case, two suitable healthy strategies with reasons, and recognition of a private route. For the exact outcome, judge emotion recognition and healthy strategy recognition separately. Help-route knowledge is recorded alongside them. Partial: feeling without clue, or strategy without fit/reason. Unobserved: no response collected, including a pass. Do not grade a learner’s own feelings or claim real-world coping from a fictional task.

“Worried means weak”: emotions are not a character grade. “Everyone shows stress the same way”: one behaviour does not establish the cause. “A pause fixes everything”: it may help when agreed with a next step; task changes or more support may still be needed. “Help is only for later”: it is available while feelings are present.

Give one precise NS: add the clue; explain how the step fits; add a second healthy way. Keep first thinking, actual access and answer prompts, one NS and reply. VF verbal feedback; WS worked with support; I independent; // self-edit; ? read back; E actual banked evidence. R only after Voice, Audience, NS and response in own colour or usual recorded mode. Offer to the Communication portfolio.

Confirm an available trusted adult before teaching. Listen calmly, avoid probing or group discussion, do not promise secrecy and follow the school’s usual procedure. Seek immediate on-site support for an urgent concern. Keep private concerns out of shared work and public evidence. The lesson is education, not treatment.

Recognise emotions and healthy ways to manage stress.

Two ways to show your thinking
Use a book or choose Type instead on the next page. An adult can read or write your words. These stories are made up.
Use story B on Support Card 2. Make a map with four parts: emotion and clue; healthy way 1 and why; healthy way 2 and why; a private help route.
Use story C on Support Card 3. Write a short note to the young person. Include the same four parts. Keep the note about the story.

1. Name the emotion and use a clue from the story. 2. Choose two healthy ways that fit the pressure. Say why each may help. 3. Give a private help route. You do not need to promise that stress will go away.
worried · frustrated · pressure · pause · plan · support

“Another way is ... . They can ask ... in private.”
They feel worried. They say they do not know where to start. One small step can make the task clear. A trusted adult can help agree what comes first. They can ask for a private talk.

This optional page is for use on screen. Choose the case map or advice note. Both have the same goal. Do not put a private personal story here.

A pass is unobserved. Record access apart from answer help. Keep first thinking and reply. E for actual work saved. R after Voice, Audience, NS and reply. Offer to the Communication portfolio.
Recognise emotions and healthy ways to manage stress.

Quote 1 worried; quote 2 frustrated. Match or identify the same words. Emotions are not moral grades. Stress describes a response to pressure, not a diagnosis from a single behaviour. A person may have more than one feeling. Use stated clues and cautious language for an inferred feeling.

Worried is stated. The pressure is organising three tasks. One manageable first step can clarify a start. Talking privately with a trusted adult can help agree priorities or adjust the demand. A request for help counts as a healthy strategy, not evidence of failure.

Both guided choices should produce two useful actions with reasons. Replace “Just do all three at once” with small steps plus adult support, or another justified pair from Card 4. The pressure may need adjusting as well as the person taking a pause.

Main B: help is available while the person still feels stressed. Parallel A: a strategy may help but more support may be needed. If incorrect or unsupported, use A’s private request and recheck privately. Keep model, word bank, frame and normal aids. No public hands-up vote.

No request for personal stress scores, symptoms, past events or family details. Do not simulate a stressful event or require breathing, eyes closed, exercise or disclosure. No clinical assessment or treatment. Generic help only. Staff confirm the actual private route before teaching.
Two choices with the same learning

Emotion: frustrated, supported by the stated quote and missed steps. Strategy 1: ask for one instruction at a time; this reduces what must be held in mind. Strategy 2: an agreed short pause with a return plan; this gives time to settle and ask for the next step. A written step list or another justified healthy pair is acceptable. Add a trusted adult/private route.

“You feel worried about speaking. Your first sentence is hard to choose. Write and rehearse one line in private so you have a clear start. Ask a trusted adult to agree support, such as a typed response, so you can take part in a suitable way. You can ask for a private talk.” Accept equivalent wording and other fitting healthy options.

Both products identify an emotion with a clue and two different healthy strategies with reasons. Each gives a private route. Book and typed work use the same checks. Scribing or an aid can capture the same thinking. Do not require a longer note or a polished diagram. A strategy’s fit matters more than its label.

Weak model: “They feel bad. Take a break.” Improve by naming worried/frustrated from a case, adding the quote, or explaining an agreed pause and return plan. Exit strategy example: “One small step may make the task clear.” Myth correction: “The person can ask for help while still feeling stressed.”

Explain a useful first step, another option and a limit. For B, a clearer instruction may address the pressure more directly than a pause alone. For C, private rehearsal may help but support or a different response mode may still be needed. Avoid ranking one route or learner as better.

Record emotion recognition and strategy recognition separately. Secure emotion recognition uses a plausible label and clue. Secure strategy recognition identifies two healthy options and links them to the pressure. Private-route knowledge is an additional recorded check. Partial evidence is retained honestly. No response, including a pass, is unobserved. Do not infer wellbeing from compliance or a completed task.

The editable Evidence Sheet includes a blank optional Type instead page. Learners may use the cells for a case map or write an advice note in its large prompt cell. Save with the usual routine and lesson code. Offer typing for either choice; a device problem should lead to book, aid or scribe access without penalty.

Read neutrally; record the learner’s exact words or selections; check back privately. Record usual access apart from answer cues. Give one NS, retain first response and reply. R follows Voice, Audience, NS and response; E means actual work saved. Offer to the Communication portfolio. Any accredited mapping needs staff confirmation.

Trusted adult and the school’s help route. A learner may point to HELP, type or write a private request, or use an aid. If one adult is busy or support is insufficient, use the route to another trusted adult. No need to exhaust self-help first. Listen calmly, avoid probing, do not promise secrecy and follow usual procedures. Keep concerns out of public evidence.
